title: Stratton Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Stratton wells have a 238 ft median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $14,300-$25,100.
h1: Stratton, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Stratton means understanding what the local well records can and cannot tell you. Permitted wells within five miles show a generally productive plains setting, with a median reported depth of 238 feet and a median reported yield of 20.0 gallons per minute. Most wells reach the Ogallala or an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. The records include older stock, irrigation, and household wells, so the right comparison depends on the intended use of the property.

This page uses Colorado DWR permit records and local cost assumptions for Stratton, with nearby context from Vona, Bethune, Seibert, Burlington, Kirk, and Flagler.

sections.heading: Stratton well depth and the local geology
sections.html:
Stratton-area wells are usually moderate-depth wells. The median reported depth is 238 feet, and the middle half runs from 200 to 250 feet. That narrow range is useful when reviewing a drilling bid: a proposal near that interval fits the local record, while a much deeper allowance deserves an explanation about the site, aquifer target, or construction plan.

Nearly all reported wells fall between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,498 feet, so local conditions are not identical on every parcel. Permits name the Ogallala on 153 wells and an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 200. Plains sedimentary rock and alluvial materials are the cost basis here, but a driller still has to confirm the formation at the actual lot.

sections.heading: What Stratton wells produce
sections.html:
Reported yields are strong overall, but the sample is smaller than the depth record: 87 wells report a pump yield. The median is 20.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 48.5 gallons per minute. That is generally more than enough production for a typical household, subject to the permit’s use limits, storage, pump sizing, and water quality.

The local record shows 89% of reported wells at 15 or more gallons per minute, 10% from 5 to 15, and 1% from 1 to 5. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. These figures are encouraging, but they are not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Ask for the well test, pump setting, recovery information, and permitted use before treating a nearby yield as your expected supply.

sections.heading: Water levels beneath Stratton
sections.html:
Only 17 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Among those records, the median depth to water is 181 feet, with the middle half from 171 to 196 feet. A buyer should use that information as a planning reference, not as a precise prediction for a new hole.

The permit history does not by itself establish a reliable long-term decline or rise in the water table. The records span the 1960s through the 2020s, but the available static measurements are too few to support a trend conclusion. Have a driller evaluate the site and ask for current neighboring water-level information. Static water level also affects pump design, electrical requirements, and the cost of getting water from the well to the house.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Stratton
sections.html:
Stratton has a long permit history. The records show permits from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2026. Activity was highest in the 2000s, when 52 permits were issued in the data, compared with 41 in the 1990s and 14 in the 2020s. Permit counts are not the same as completed wells, so they should not be read as current market share.

The most active names in these records are Schaal Drilling Co. (Schaal, Ruben T.) with 69 wells, Parrish Drilling (Parrish, Wayne) with 22, and Klassen Drilling (Klassen, Paul C) with 11. Contact current licensed drillers for access review, a site-specific estimate, casing and grout details, pump sizing, and a realistic dry-hole or insufficient-yield plan.

sections.heading: What a new Stratton well may cost
sections.html:
For Stratton’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the modeled drilling rate is $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 238 feet, that places the drilled hole at about $8,300 to $13,100. This is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $14,300 to $25,100. The final bid can move with access, casing and grout requirements, pump depth, power availability, trench length, and whether the hole must go deeper than the local norm. Compare bids line by line. Confirm what testing, permits, abandonment protection, electrical work, and connection to the proposed home are included rather than comparing only the per-foot figure.

sections.heading: Stratton risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Yield is a favorable part of the local record, but the database still has gaps: 147 wells are recorded as constructed, 207 report total depth, and 87 report pump yield. A permit or a nearby productive well does not guarantee the same result on your parcel. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable, and a dry hole or low-yield result remains a construction risk even in a strong area.

Water quality deserves separate attention. Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about ten miles, with no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites listed. Test an existing well before purchase and test a new well after construction. Check septic setbacks, soil conditions, building access, and the space needed for a septic system, driveway, utilities, and future repairs. DWR rules control the permitted use; an exempt household-use well is not unrestricted, and the general exempt-well pumping limit is 35 gallons per minute.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Stratton
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not a countywide assumption. Pull the DWR permit, well construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and recorded use for the property. Compare those documents with neighboring wells in Stratton, Vona, Bethune, Seibert, Burlington, Kirk, and Flagler where relevant. The local depth and yield statistics support a reasonable feasibility conversation, but they do not replace a site-specific review.

For a vacant lot, make the well location, drilling access, septic area, driveway route, and electrical path part of the early layout. Ask a driller for a written bid based on the local 200-to-250-foot middle range, while allowing for deeper conditions. If the parcel is in an over-appropriated basin, confirm whether an augmentation plan or another water-right arrangement is required. Make the purchase contract contingent on satisfactory water quantity, quality, and legal-use review.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Stratton, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Stratton is 238 feet. The middle half runs from 200 to 250 feet, and 98% of reported depths are between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest record is 1,498 feet, so a site-specific bid can still differ substantially from the local norm.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Stratton?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate for Stratton’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 238-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,300 to $13,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $14,300 to $25,100.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Stratton?
faq.a: Among the 87 local wells that report a pump yield, the median is 20.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 15.0 to 48.5 gallons per minute. Reported yields show 89% at 15 or more gallons per minute, but a neighboring well does not guarantee the same result on a new parcel.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Stratton?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from well depth or yield. Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about ten miles of Stratton, so test an existing well before buying and test a new well after construction. Review the complete laboratory report and use a qualified professional to interpret results for household drinking water.

faq.q: Are Stratton wells affected by a falling water table?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a dependable rise or decline. Only 17 wells report static water levels. Their median depth to water is 181 feet, with the middle half from 171 to 196 feet. Those measurements are useful for planning, but too limited to prove a long-term trend at a specific Stratton property.
